notes.front: In Subpart F, what is a safety can?
notes.back: An approved closed container of up to 5 gallons, with flash-arresting screen, spring-closing lid and spout cover, that relieves internal pressure in a fire.
notes.explanation: Each feature is part of the definition, so an ordinary closed can does not qualify.
notes.example: Like a household fuel can, but approved, with a spring lid that snaps shut and a screen to stop flame getting inside.
notes.evidence: Safety can means an approved closed container, of not more than 5 gallons capacity, having a flash-arresting screen, spring-closing lid and spout cover and so designed that it will safely relieve internal pressure when subjected to fire exposure.

notes.front: In Subpart F, what is a flammable liquid?
notes.back: A liquid with a vapour pressure not above 40 psi (absolute) at 100 °F and a flashpoint at or below 199.4 °F (93 °C).
notes.explanation: The definition rests on two measured properties, and such liquids are then split into four categories by flashpoint and boiling point.
notes.example: Like petrol or many solvent-based thinners on site, judged by their flashpoint rather than by how they smell.
notes.evidence: Flammable liquid means any liquid having a vapor pressure not exceeding 40 pounds per square inch (absolute) at 100 °F (37.8 °C) and having a flashpoint at or below 199.4 °F (93 °C).

notes.front: What is a fire watch, as described in 1926.352(e)?
notes.back: Additional personnel assigned to guard against fire during welding, cutting or heating and for long enough afterwards to ensure no possibility of fire.
notes.explanation: It is required where normal fire prevention precautions are not sufficient for the operation.
notes.example: Like a lifeguard for hot work: someone whose job is to watch for fire rather than to do the welding.
notes.evidence: When the welding, cutting, or heating operation is such that normal fire prevention precautions are not sufficient, additional personnel shall be assigned to guard against fire while the actual welding, cutting, or heating operation is being performed, and for a sufficient period of time after completion of the work

notes.front: Who must develop the construction fire protection programme, and for how long must it be followed?
notes.back: The employer, throughout all phases of the construction and demolition work.
notes.explanation: The same paragraph adds that, as fire hazards occur, there shall be no delay in providing the necessary equipment.
notes.evidence: The employer shall be responsible for the development of a fire protection program to be followed throughout all phases of the construction and demolition work,

notes.front: Timber formwork starts piling up on a site that has no firefighting equipment yet. The manager plans to buy extinguishers at the end of the month. What does 1926.150 say?
notes.back: A: there must be no delay in providing the necessary equipment as fire hazards occur.
notes.choices:
A) There must be no delay in providing the necessary equipment as fire hazards occur
B) End of the month is acceptable
C) Equipment is needed only once the building is enclosed
D) Only a written plan is needed, not equipment
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: the rule allows no delay once hazards occur. D is wrong: the employer must also provide the firefighting equipment.
notes.explanation: Equipment must follow the hazard straight away, not a later purchasing date.
notes.evidence: As fire hazards occur, there shall be no delay in providing the necessary equipment.

notes.front: What must happen to the firefighting equipment the employer provides on a construction site?
notes.back: It must be conspicuously located, accessible at all times, periodically inspected and kept in operating condition.
notes.explanation: Defective equipment must be replaced immediately, so a faulty extinguisher cannot be left in place.
notes.evidence: (4) All firefighting equipment shall be periodically inspected and maintained in operating condition. Defective equipment shall be immediately replaced.

notes.front: A fire extinguisher rated not less than 2A must be provided for each {{c1::3,000}} square feet of the protected building area, or major fraction thereof.
notes.explanation: The rating and the floor area work together: the bigger the protected area, the more 2A units are needed.
notes.evidence: A fire extinguisher, rated not less than 2A, shall be provided for each 3,000 square feet of the protected building area, or major fraction thereof.

notes.front: A single-storey building under construction has 9,000 square feet of protected area. What is the minimum number of 2A-rated extinguishers?
notes.back: B: three.
notes.choices:
A) One
B) Three
C) Nine
D) None, if a hose is on site
notes.choicesExplained: A and C misapply the 3,000 square feet ratio. D is wrong: a hose line can substitute only if it meets the stated conditions, not simply by being on site.
notes.explanation: One 2A extinguisher is required for each 3,000 square feet, and 9,000 is three times that.
notes.evidence: A fire extinguisher, rated not less than 2A, shall be provided for each 3,000 square feet of the protected building area,

notes.front: Travel distance from any point of the protected area to the nearest fire extinguisher shall not exceed {{c1::100}} feet.
notes.explanation: This limit applies alongside the 2A-per-3,000-square-feet rule, so placement matters as well as numbers.
notes.evidence: Travel distance from any point of the protected area to the nearest fire extinguisher shall not exceed 100 feet.

notes.front: A site has enough 2A extinguishers for its floor area, but all are in one store, 130 feet from the far end of the building. Is that compliant?
notes.back: B: no; travel distance to the nearest extinguisher must not exceed 100 feet.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the number of units is what counts
B) No; travel distance to the nearest extinguisher must not exceed 100 feet
C) Yes, if the building is under 10,000 square feet
D) Yes, if the store is unlocked
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C ignore the travel-distance limit, which applies from any point of the protected area.
notes.explanation: Meeting the number of units does not satisfy the separate travel-distance limit.
notes.evidence: Travel distance from any point of the protected area to the nearest fire extinguisher shall not exceed 100 feet.

notes.front: What may be substituted for a fire extinguisher having a 2A rating?
notes.back: One 55-gallon open drum of water with two fire pails, or a qualifying ½-inch garden-type hose line.
notes.explanation: The hose must not exceed 100 feet, must have a nozzle and must discharge at least 5 gallons per minute.
notes.evidence: (ii) One 55-gallon open drum of water with two fire pails may be substituted for a fire extinguisher having a 2A rating.

notes.front: What containers must be used for handling and using flammable liquids in quantities of 5 gallons or less?
notes.back: Approved safety cans or Department of Transportation approved containers.
notes.explanation: Highly viscid liquids may stay in their original shipping containers, and one gallon or less may stay in the original container.
notes.evidence: Approved safety cans or Department of Transportation approved containers shall be used for the handling and use of flammable liquids in quantities of 5 gallons or less,

notes.front: A labourer carries 3 gallons of petrol to a saw in an old open-topped paint bucket. What does 1926.152 require instead?
notes.back: C: an approved safety can or a Department of Transportation approved container.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as small amounts are exempt
B) A lid on the bucket
C) An approved safety can or a Department of Transportation approved container
D) A glass bottle
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rule is for quantities of 5 gallons or less. B and D are not approved containers.
notes.explanation: Quantities of 5 gallons or less must be handled in approved safety cans or approved transport containers.
notes.evidence: Approved safety cans or Department of Transportation approved containers shall be used for the handling and use of flammable liquids in quantities of 5 gallons or less,

notes.front: Where must flammable liquids never be stored?
notes.back: In areas used for exits or stairways, or normally used for the safe passage of people.
notes.explanation: The rule protects routes people rely on to pass safely, including exits and stairways.
notes.evidence: Flammable liquids shall not be stored in areas used for exits, stairways, or normally used for the safe passage of people.

notes.front: No more than {{c1::25}} gallons of flammable liquids shall be stored in a room outside an approved storage cabinet.
notes.explanation: Larger quantities must go into an acceptable or approved cabinet.
notes.evidence: No more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids shall be stored in a room outside of an approved storage cabinet.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.152, Flammable liquids(b)(1), Indoor storage, p. 174

notes.front: How far from an outside flammable liquid storage area must a 20-B extinguisher be located?
notes.back: Not less than 25 feet, nor more than 75 feet, from the storage area.
notes.explanation: The rule sets both a minimum and a maximum distance, so an extinguisher right beside the store does not comply.
notes.evidence: At least one portable fire extinguisher having a rating of not less than 20–B units shall be located not less than 25 feet, nor more than 75 feet, from any flammable liquid storage area located outside.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.152, Flammable liquids(d)(2), Fire control, p. 176

notes.front: What sign must be posted where smoking is prohibited near operations that are a fire hazard?
notes.back: "No Smoking or Open Flame", conspicuously posted.
notes.explanation: Smoking is prohibited at or near such operations, and the sign makes the ban visible.
notes.evidence: Smoking shall be prohibited at or in the vicinity of operations which constitute a fire hazard, and shall be conspicuously posted: ‘‘No Smoking or Open Flame.’’

notes.front: What must be provided when temporary heaters are used, and what if natural fresh air is inadequate?
notes.back: Fresh air in sufficient quantities for workers' health and safety; mechanical ventilation where natural supply is inadequate.
notes.explanation: In confined spaces, special care is needed to ensure proper combustion and limit temperature rise.
notes.evidence: Fresh air shall be supplied in sufficient quantities to maintain the health and safety of workmen. Where natural means of fresh air supply is inadequate, mechanical ventilation shall be provided.

notes.front: What must be in place and secured when compressed gas cylinders are transported, moved or stored?
notes.back: Valve protection caps.
notes.explanation: This is the first rule listed for transporting, moving and storing cylinders.
notes.evidence: (a) Transporting, moving, and storing compressed gas cylinders. (1) Valve protection caps shall be in place and secured.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(1), p. 213

notes.front: How must cylinders be hoisted, and what must never be used to hoist them?
notes.back: Secured on a cradle, slingboard or pallet; never by magnets or choker slings.
notes.explanation: When moved by hand, they are tilted and rolled on their bottom edges, not dropped or struck.
notes.evidence: When cylinders are hoisted, they shall be secured on a cradle, slingboard, or pallet. They shall not be hoisted or transported by means of magnets or choker slings.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(2), p. 213

notes.front: A crane crew plans to lift a bundle of acetylene cylinders to the roof with a choker sling, caps removed to save weight. What is wrong?
notes.back: C: caps must be in place and secured, and cylinders go up on a cradle, slingboard or pallet, not a choker.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the sling is rated
B) Only the caps
C) Caps must be in place and secured, and cylinders go up on a cradle, slingboard or pallet, not a choker
D) Only the sling; caps are optional when lifting
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores both rules. B and D each fix only half of the problem.
notes.explanation: Both parts of the plan break the transport rules for cylinders.
notes.evidence: (1) Valve protection caps shall be in place and secured. (2) When cylinders are hoisted, they shall be secured on a cradle, slingboard, or pallet. They shall not be hoisted or transported by means of magnets or choker slings.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(1)–(2), p. 213

notes.front: In what position must compressed gas cylinders be secured?
notes.back: Upright at all times, except if necessary for short periods while actually being hoisted or carried.
notes.explanation: A cylinder truck, chain or other steadying device keeps cylinders from being knocked over while in use.
notes.evidence: Compressed gas cylinders shall be secured in an upright position at all times except, if necessary, for short periods of time while cylinders are actually being hoisted or carried.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(9), p. 214

notes.front: At the end of a shift, a welder lays an oxygen cylinder on its side under a bench overnight. Is that allowed?
notes.back: C: no; cylinders must be secured upright except briefly while actually being hoisted or carried.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the valve is closed
B) Yes, under a bench it is protected
C) No; cylinders must be secured upright except briefly while actually being hoisted or carried
D) Yes, oxygen cylinders are exempt
notes.choicesExplained: A and B do not meet the upright rule. D is wrong: the rule covers compressed gas cylinders generally.
notes.explanation: Overnight storage is not a short period of hoisting or carrying, so the upright rule applies.
notes.evidence: Compressed gas cylinders shall be secured in an upright position at all times except, if necessary, for short periods of time while cylinders are actually being hoisted or carried.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(9), p. 214

notes.front: How must stored oxygen cylinders be separated from fuel-gas cylinders or combustibles?
notes.back: By at least 20 feet, or by a non-combustible barrier at least 5 feet high with at least a half-hour fire-resistance rating.
notes.explanation: The rule names oil and grease as combustibles of particular concern.
notes.evidence: Oxygen cylinders in storage shall be separated from fuel-gas cylinders or combustible materials (especially oil or grease), a minimum distance of 20 feet (6.1 m) or by a noncombustible barrier at least 5 feet (1.5 m) high having a fire-resistance rating of at least onehalf hour.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(10), p. 214

notes.front: In a storage cage, oxygen cylinders stand 8 feet from acetylene cylinders with nothing between them. Which change would comply?
notes.back: A: move them at least 20 feet apart, or put up a qualifying non-combustible barrier.
notes.choices:
A) Move them at least 20 feet apart, or put up a qualifying non-combustible barrier
B) Move them 10 feet apart
C) Put a tarpaulin between them
D) Chain them together
notes.choicesExplained: D does not separate them. B is short of 20 feet. C is not a non-combustible, fire-rated barrier.
notes.explanation: Separation can be by distance or by a 5-foot barrier with at least a half-hour fire-resistance rating.
notes.evidence: a minimum distance of 20 feet (6.1 m) or by a noncombustible barrier at least 5 feet (1.5 m) high having a fire-resistance rating of at least onehalf hour.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting(a)(10), p. 214

notes.front: Before welding, cutting or heating, what should happen to the object or to nearby fire hazards?
notes.back: When practical, move the object to a safe location; if it cannot be moved, take movable fire hazards to a safe place or protect them.
notes.explanation: If neither is possible, positive means must confine the heat, sparks and slag.
notes.evidence: When practical, objects to be welded, cut, or heated shall be moved to a designated safe location or, if the objects to be welded, cut, or heated cannot be readily moved, all movable fire hazards in the vicinity shall be taken to a safe place, or otherwise protected.

notes.front: Besides the hot work itself, for how long must the fire watch continue?
notes.back: For a sufficient period after the work is completed to ensure no possibility of fire exists.
notes.explanation: The personnel must also be told the specific fire hazards expected and how to use the firefighting equipment.
notes.evidence: and for a sufficient period of time after completion of the work to ensure that no possibility of fire exists. Such personnel shall be instructed as to the specific anticipated fire hazards and how the firefighting equipment provided is to be used.

notes.front: In underground construction, when must a fire watch be maintained?
notes.back: When hot work is performed.
notes.explanation: The underground rule points back to the fire watch described in 1926.352(e).
notes.evidence: A fire watch as described in § 1926.352(e) shall be maintained when hot work is performed.

notes.front: Normal precautions are not enough for cutting steel beside timber. The cutter finishes and the fire watch leaves at once for lunch. What is wrong?
notes.back: A: the watch must stay long enough after completion to ensure no possibility of fire.
notes.choices:
A) The watch must stay long enough after completion to ensure no possibility of fire
B) Nothing: the watch ends when cutting stops
C) The cutter should have been the fire watch
D) A fire watch is only needed underground
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the period after completion. C is wrong: the rule assigns additional personnel. D is wrong: 1926.352(e) applies to welding, cutting and heating generally.
notes.explanation: The fire watch covers the work and a sufficient period after it.
notes.evidence: additional personnel shall be assigned to guard against fire while the actual welding, cutting, or heating operation is being performed, and for a sufficient period of time after completion of the work to ensure that no possibility of fire exists.

notes.front: When is welding, cutting or heating prohibited outright under 1926.352(c)?
notes.back: Where flammable paints, other flammable compounds or heavy dust concentrations create a hazard.
notes.explanation: This paragraph is a flat prohibition, whereas paragraphs (a) and (b) deal with moving or shielding fire hazards.
notes.evidence: No welding, cutting, or heating shall be done where the application of flammable paints, or the presence of other flammable compounds, or heavy dust concentrations creates a hazard.

notes.front: How is the shade of a welding filter lens chosen, and may a darker one be used?
notes.back: Table E-1 is the guide; shades more dense than those listed may be used to suit the individual.
notes.explanation: The table is described as a guide, so it sets a starting point rather than a single fixed shade.
notes.evidence: Table E–1 shall be used as a guide for the selection of the proper shade numbers of filter lenses or plates used in welding. Shades more dense than those listed may be used to suit the individual’s needs.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.102(c)(1), Protection against radiant energy, p. 169

notes.front: What does 1926.351 say about arc welding cables in need of repair, and about worn cable exposing bare conductors?
notes.back: Cables in need of repair shall not be used; a worn portion exposing bare conductors must be protected with rubber and friction tape or equivalent.
notes.explanation: The first sentence bars cable in need of repair outright; the second deals with wear that exposes conductors.
notes.evidence: Cables in need of repair shall not be used. When a cable, other than the cable lead referred to in paragraph (b)(2) of this section, becomes worn to the extent of exposing bare conductors, the portion thus exposed shall be protected by means of rubber and friction tape or other equivalent insulation.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.351(b)(4), Arc welding and cutting, p. 216
